content.text: With more letters, guessing gets hard. Work backward: find the ways the conclusion can be false, then check whether one of them also makes every premise true.

content.definition: Truth values for the letters that make every premise true and the conclusion false.

examples.title: A search that succeeds
lines: The argument: (P → Q) → R, P → R, so P → Q.
The conclusion is false only when P is true and Q is false.
P → R then needs R true.
(P → Q) → R is then false → true, which is true.
examples.conclusion: Countermodel: P true, Q false, R true.

examples.title: A search that fails
lines: The argument: P → Q, P, so Q.
The conclusion is false only when Q is false.
Then P → Q needs P false, but the premise P needs P true.
examples.conclusion: No row works, so the argument is valid.

question.prompt: Where should a search for a countermodel start?
question.hint: A countermodel needs one thing from the conclusion.
question.explanation: A countermodel makes the conclusion false. Start there, then try to make the premises true.
